Tracing Messages API requests and Managed Agents sessions

Claude Code and the Agent SDK export OpenTelemetry metrics, log events and traces from the process that runs them. That covers one client at a time. Watching a whole organisation takes four further streams, each answering a different question: spans emitted by the Claude API itself, the usage and cost of individual Managed Agents sessions, organisation-wide usage and cost reports, and adoption and audit records. This page covers each in turn. A Managed Agents session is a run of an agent on the Claude Platform, with its own threads, tools and usage totals, which you can inspect in the Claude Console.

Client-side telemetry stops at your process boundary. The Claude API can emit its own spans, one for each model request and each tool use it runs on Messages API requests and Managed Agents sessions, without any code change. You receive them by adding a
destination

: an OTLP/HTTP endpoint that accepts protobuf over HTTPS on port 443, plus the headers that authenticate to it. Only organisation admins can add or change destinations. A destination covers All workspaces, Selected ones, or All except a list. Its content mode is either Metadata only or Full content. That is the same opt-in idea as in Claude Code, which redacts prompt, response and tool content by default and records it only when you switch it on.

On their own, API spans start their own traces. To nest them under your application's spans, call the SDK from inside one of your own spans. The SDK writes a W3C

header, and your sampler controls its sampled flag. When the flag is off, the API emits no spans for that request. The same propagation continues into MCP servers connected through the MCP connector, which receive a
in
and can attach their own spans.

Delivery is at least once and best effort. Expect duplicate spans and deduplicate on trace ID plus span ID. A lost span is never resent. The Console's Delivery column shows Healthy, Failing, No data or Disabled. The API disables a destination that answers with a 3xx redirect, resolves to a non-public IP, or fails every delivery for 24 hours.
Exam trap
Every Messages API request sent to a workspace covered by a destination produces spans.
Why is that wrong?

An organisation has a destination covering all workspaces. Their application calls the SDK inside its own spans, and its sampler keeps only 10% of traces. What happens to the API spans for the other 90% of Messages API requests?

Usage and cost of a Managed Agents session
A single Managed Agents session reports its own consumption. The session object's
field holds cumulative token counts, cache reads and writes, server tool requests,
and

. A session can run several threads, for example one per agent in a multiagent session, and the Console's session viewer shows one timeline lane per thread, a transcript, and a Tools tab with failure counts and median duration.
is the time during which at least one thread was running, with overlapping threads counted once. The session's running-time cost is priced on that duration. Each thread also reports its own
, but per-thread costs are rounded independently and leave out the running-time cost, so the session figure is the authoritative one.

event carries the same cumulative snapshot on the session stream, so you don't have to poll. It is emitted on idle transitions rather than on a timer: immediately before the session goes idle, and when a thread pauses at a session budget. During a long run you therefore see no new totals until one of those moments. That is why a spend cap built from watching usage and stopping the session yourself fails, since the stop arrives after the money is spent. A session budget is a dollar cap on list cost. The platform prices consumption continuously and pauses each thread before its next model request once the cap is reached, so enforcement doesn't depend on your code noticing in time.
Checkpoint 3 of 6
Check yourself
Your team runs long Managed Agents sessions and must make sure none of them goes past a fixed dollar amount at list price. Which approach should you build?
Subscribe to session.usage events and stop the session once list_cost passes the limit
Set a session budget on each session
Add up each thread's list_cost from the Threads tab and stop the session when the total hits the limit
Poll the session object every few seconds and stop the session when list_cost reaches the limit

Usage & Cost Admin API: organisation-wide trends

The Usage & Cost Admin API answers organisation-wide questions: tokens by model, workspace, API key or service tier over time, and spend by day. You call it with an Admin API key. The response is a series of time buckets, and
sets their granularity. Each width has its own default and maximum
, which is the number of buckets returned per request. The cost endpoint offers only daily buckets.
Predict first
During an incident you want to spot token spikes as fast as possible using the usage endpoint. What polling rate gives the freshest picture?
Every few seconds with 1m buckets, since faster polling surfaces spikes sooner
Once an hour with 1h buckets, since hourly buckets refresh every minute
About once a minute with 1m buckets, since data lands minutes after requests complete

Checkpoint 5 of 6
Exam question

During an active incident, an on-call engineer needs a near real-time view of organization-wide token consumption spikes, checking for anomalies roughly once a minute. Which Usage API configuration fits this monitoring need within the documented granularity limits?
Request bucket_width=1m, raise the limit above the 60-bucket default up to the 1440-bucket maximum as needed, and poll about once per minute
Request bucket_width=1d with the default 7-bucket limit, since daily granularity is sufficient to detect minute-level spikes retroactively
Request bucket_width=1h with the 168-bucket maximum limit, since hourly buckets update automatically every 60 seconds
Request bucket_width=1m but poll every 5 seconds to catch spikes as soon as they occur, since finer polling improves data freshness

Adoption analytics, audit events and SIEM routing

Spend data shows what Claude Code costs. Adoption data shows whether people use it. The Claude Code analytics dashboard reports usage metrics: lines of code accepted, suggestion accept rate, and daily active users and sessions. Teams and Enterprise plans add contribution metrics from a GitHub integration, such as merged PRs that contain Claude Code lines, plus a leaderboard and CSV export. On API organisations the dashboard lives in the Claude Console and adds spend tracking and team insights.

Administrative actions are a different stream again. The compliance activities endpoint lets you query actions such as workspaces being created or archived, members being added or removed, RBAC custom roles being created or assigned, spend limits being changed, and the zero data retention override being toggled. It also logs reads: viewing the Claude Code usage report or the messages usage report is itself an activity.

Claude Code's per-user activity reaches a retention store such as a SIEM through the logs exporter. Managed settings are the policy settings an admin deploys and enforces across all Claude Code users, so they are the right place for this configuration. When managed settings set an endpoint or credential, Claude Code removes any per-signal endpoints a developer set, so a developer can't send logs to a different collector. Three switches matter here.
